arguments.title: How to prepare your bike before a puncture repair visit
arguments.excerpt: A short preparation checklist for bike owners: what to notice about the air loss, and what to bring when you drop the bike at our workshop for puncture repair.

arguments.content:
A flat tire is easier to sort out when you arrive with a clear picture of what happened. Our workshop repairs bicycle tire punctures and inspects tires, and one of the most useful things you can bring along is a short description of when the air loss occurs. Here is how to put that description together before you visit.

Notice when the air disappears

Air loss follows patterns, and the pattern tells us where to look. Before you head over, think about which of these fits your bike:

  • The tire went flat suddenly while you were riding.
  • The tire goes soft over a few hours after you pump it.
  • The tire holds air for several days, then needs topping up again.
  • The tire only loses air after you ride over rough ground or a kerb.

Write your answer down or keep it in a note on your phone. A sentence such as "it stays firm overnight but is soft by the evening" is more useful to us than "it keeps going flat".

Note where and how you were riding

If the flat arrived during a ride, try to recall the surface: broken glass on a road, a gravel path, a building site, or a hard kerb strike. If you have had several flats on the same wheel in a short period, mention that too. Repeat punctures on one wheel point somewhere different from a single unlucky ride.

Leave the evidence in place

It is tempting to pull the tire off and hunt for the hole yourself. If you would rather leave it to us, the most helpful thing is to leave the wheel and tire as they are. The position of the object in the tread, and how the tube sits inside the tire, are both clues. If you have already removed the tube or patched it, keep the old tube and bring it with you.

What to bring with the bike

You can bring the bike in and describe the problem at the counter. A few extras help:

  • The whole bike, rather than just the wheel, if you are not sure which wheel is affected.
  • Any tube you already removed or patched.
  • Anything you pulled out of the tire, such as a thorn, tack or shard.
  • Your lock or accessories removed if they get in the way of the wheel.

A quick check before you leave home

Pump the tire up and give it a minute. If it is soft again immediately, say so. If it stays hard and only fails after a ride, say that instead. Either observation narrows things down, and both are quicker to gather at home than in the workshop.

Bring the description, we will do the rest

None of this asks you to diagnose the puncture. The aim is simply that when you arrive, you can answer one question clearly: when does the air go? With that, we can inspect the tire and get on with the repair. You can read what the service covers on our bicycle puncture repair page.
